name: Nimacimab

angle.text: Nimacimab is an experimental anti-CB1 antibody that fat-loss followers track as a peripherally acting obesity drug. It is in Phase 2 for obesity; any use for appearance is untested.

summary: An experimental anti-CB1 antibody for obesity that is still in Phase 2, with no appearance-use evidence.
note: Investigational only; no approved use and no published obesity results found.
currentQuick:
Nimacimab is an antibody drug that blocks the cannabinoid-1 receptor, a target involved in appetite and metabolism. It is being studied for obesity, including alongside semaglutide.
It remains experimental. The registered obesity trial began in 2024, and no published efficacy results were found.
How it works: It binds CB1 from outside the cell. Researchers designed it to work mainly in peripheral tissue so that it avoids the psychiatric effects seen with earlier brain-penetrant CB1 blockers.
Risks and caveats: Its safety profile is not established in published form. It is not approved anywhere and is available only within clinical trials.
deepLead:
Nimacimab is an investigational monoclonal antibody that targets the cannabinoid-1 receptor (CB1) and is being developed for obesity and other metabolic conditions. Unlike earlier small-molecule CB1 blockers, it is designed to act on peripheral tissues rather than the brain, with the aim of avoiding the neuropsychiatric side effects that ended earlier drugs in this class.
It has been registered in human trials in at least two settings: a small Phase 2 study in diabetic gastroparesis that began in 2019, and a Phase 2 obesity trial that began in 2024 and tests weekly nimacimab alone and together with semaglutide against placebo. Published results from the obesity trial were not available in the sources reviewed for this article.
Nimacimab is not an approved medicine and is not an established part of appearance or fat-loss practice. It appears in this wiki because of interest in new anti-obesity drug targets.

name: NAD+ injections

angle.text: Injected NAD+ is promoted by longevity clinics and online communities as an anti-aging and energy treatment, with users hoping for fresher skin and a more youthful look. The appearance claim rests on cell biology and anecdote; controlled human trials for aging or looks are lacking.

summary: Injected NAD+ is sold as a longevity and energy treatment, but no controlled human trials support it for aging or appearance.
note: Long-term safety of IV NAD+ is described as unknown; not licensed as a medicine in the UK.
currentQuick:
NAD+ is a coenzyme every cell uses for metabolism. Some clinics sell injections or infusions of it for anti-aging, energy and recovery.
The molecule is well understood, but no controlled human trial of injected NAD+ for appearance or healthy aging was found. Registered trials address specific medical conditions.
How it works: NAD+ carries electrons in metabolic reactions and is used by sirtuin, PARP and CD38 enzymes. Proponents say injecting it raises levels that fall with age; reference sources note that human evidence for that decline is inconsistent.
Risks and caveats: Experts quoted in reference works say long-term safety of IV NAD+ is unknown. It is not licensed as a medicine in the UK, and clinic marketing claims have not been tested in controlled trials.
deepLead:
NAD+ injections are parenteral (injected or infused) preparations of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a coenzyme found in all living cells. They are marketed by some wellness and longevity clinics, and discussed online, as an anti-aging or energy-boosting treatment.
NAD+ itself is a well-characterised molecule central to cellular metabolism. The claim that raising NAD+ by injection slows aging or improves appearance is a separate question, and no controlled human trial of injected NAD+ for appearance or aging was found. Registered human trials of injectable NAD+ (often called coenzyme I in Chinese registrations) address other conditions, such as hematopoietic recovery, hearing loss and vascular aging.
In the United Kingdom, NAD+ is not licensed as a medicine, and experts quoted in reference works say the long-term safety of intravenous NAD+ is unknown.

name: Glutathione injections

angle.text: Injected glutathione, often paired with vitamin C, is used in some countries and online communities to lighten skin and even out tone. Evidence for skin lightening comes from small studies of mixed quality; its effectiveness is unclear.

summary: Injected glutathione is used for skin lightening, but its effectiveness is unclear and the Philippine government advises against IV use.
note: Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione; efficacy unclear as of a 2019 review.
currentQuick:
Glutathione is an antioxidant peptide the body makes. Some clinics and online communities use injections or IV drips of it to lighten skin.
Reference works describe its effectiveness for skin whitening as unclear as of 2019. No controlled trial of injected glutathione for general skin lightening was found.
How it works: Proponents say glutathione reduces melanin production, and that injection avoids poor oral absorption. Reference sources confirm oral absorption is poor but do not establish the lightening mechanism.
Risks and caveats: The Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione because of possible side effects. No controlled safety data for cosmetic injection were found.
deepLead:
Glutathione (GSH) is a small tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine and glycine that cells produce naturally and use as a major antioxidant. Intravenous or intramuscular glutathione is promoted in some countries and online communities as a skin-lightening treatment, often alongside vitamin C.
Reference works state that whether glutathione actually lightens skin was unclear as of 2019, citing a systematic review, and that the Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione because of possible side effects. No controlled clinical trial of injected glutathione for general skin lightening was found among the study records reviewed for this article.

name: VIP (Vasoactive intestinal peptide)

angle.text: VIP is a natural vasodilating neuropeptide sold as a research peptide, and users speculate it could aid recovery and circulation. No human studies address any appearance use; its established research concerns gut, lung and immune function.

summary: A natural vasodilating neuropeptide sold as a research peptide, with no human evidence for any appearance use.
note: Human studies are small physiology or headache-provocation trials; not studied for appearance.
currentQuick:
VIP is a natural 28-amino-acid peptide that widens blood vessels, relaxes smooth muscle and modulates immune activity. Some vendors list it as a research peptide.
Human trials of VIP are small and aimed at physiology, headache or lung disease. None tests it for appearance or recovery.
How it works: It binds VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP in target cells. Its half-life in blood is about two minutes.
Risks and caveats: Intravenous VIP was used in migraine studies to provoke headache, showing it can have vascular effects. No safety data exist for the research-peptide use pattern.
deepLead:
Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) is a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide found in the gut, brain, heart, lungs and other tissues. It acts through the VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors and has vasodilating, smooth-muscle-relaxing and immune-modulating effects.
VIP is sold online in some peptide markets as a research compound. Published human research on injected VIP itself is limited to small physiological and headache-provocation studies, a Phase 1 study in respiratory distress, and trials of its synthetic form aviptadil. No study of VIP for appearance was found.

name: Aviptadil

chain: Used for erectile function and lung disease
angle.text: Aviptadil is synthetic VIP used with phentolamine as an injection for erectile dysfunction in some European countries and tested in COVID-19 lung failure. Peptide communities mention it alongside VIP for circulation and recovery; no appearance use has been studied.

summary: Synthetic VIP used for erectile dysfunction and tested in COVID-19 lung failure; no appearance evidence.
note: Investigational for lung disease; large COVID-19 trial reported no significant benefit.
currentQuick:
Aviptadil is a lab-made version of vasoactive intestinal peptide. In some countries it is approved, with phentolamine, as an injection for erectile dysfunction.
It was also tested for COVID-19 respiratory failure; a reference summary says the large TESICO trial showed no significant benefit. It has no studied role in appearance.
How it works: It activates VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, producing vasodilation and anti-inflammatory effects. Preclinical work suggested effects on lung surfactant and cytokines.
Risks and caveats: Safety data come from patient trials in erectile dysfunction and critical illness. It is not approved for lung disease in the US, and no data exist for healthy-use contexts.
deepLead:
Aviptadil is a synthetic form of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide first characterised in 1970. It has been used as an injectable in combination with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction in some European countries, and it has been studied as an intravenous or inhaled treatment for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pulmonary hypertension and COVID-19 respiratory failure.
The largest randomized test, the TESICO trial in COVID-19 respiratory failure, was published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine in 2023; a reference summary states that it showed no significant improvement in outcomes versus placebo. Aviptadil is not approved for any lung indication in the US.
It appears in this wiki because the parent peptide, VIP, is sold as a research compound. No study of aviptadil for appearance or recovery in healthy people was found.

name: Ara-290

angle.text: ARA 290 is an EPO-derived repair peptide that recovery-focused users discuss for tissue protection and nerve healing. It has been tested in small neuropathy trials; use for recovery or appearance in healthy people is untested.

summary: An EPO-derived repair peptide tested in small neuropathy trials, with no data for appearance or recovery in healthy people.
note: Investigational; human data limited to small trials in sarcoidosis and diabetes neuropathy.
currentQuick:
ARA 290 (cibinetide) is a short peptide derived from erythropoietin, designed to trigger tissue-protective signalling without boosting red blood cells.
It has been studied in small trials for nerve pain and nerve-fibre loss in sarcoidosis and diabetes. It has not been tested for appearance or recovery in healthy people.
How it works: It is designed to activate the innate repair receptor, which researchers describe as mediating tissue protection and anti-inflammation, while avoiding the hematologic effects of EPO.
Risks and caveats: Safety data come from small patient trials. It is investigational and has no approved use.
deepLead:
ARA 290, also known as cibinetide, is an 11-amino-acid peptide engineered from the structure of erythropoietin (EPO). It was designed to activate the innate repair receptor involved in tissue protection without raising red blood cell counts, avoiding the thrombosis risk associated with recombinant EPO.
It was developed by Araim Pharmaceuticals and has been tested in small human trials of neuropathic symptoms in sarcoidosis and type 2 diabetes. Authors of these studies reported symptom and nerve-fibre improvements, but the trials were small and exploratory. No study of ARA 290 for appearance was found.

name: B7-33

angle.text: B7-33 is a lab-made relaxin mimic studied in animals for fibrosis, and peptide communities speculate about it for tissue repair and scar reduction. There are no human trials and no documented appearance use.

summary: A lab-made relaxin mimic studied in animals for fibrosis; no human trials and no documented appearance use.
note: Preclinical only; no human safety or efficacy data.
currentQuick:
B7-33 is a short peptide designed to imitate part of the hormone relaxin-2, which has anti-fibrotic and blood-vessel-relaxing effects. It was built because the natural hormone is expensive to make.
All published findings are from cells, mice and rats, mainly on heart and kidney fibrosis. No human trial exists, and no source reviewed describes appearance-related use.
How it works: It binds the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is biased, activating ERK1/2 signalling more than cAMP, according to the research that characterised it.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unstudied. It is not an approved drug anywhere; availability is limited to research-chemical channels.
deepLead:
B7-33 is a laboratory-designed, single-chain peptide derived from the B-chain of human relaxin-2, a pleiotropic hormone with vasodilatory and anti-fibrotic properties. It was engineered as a simpler and cheaper mimic of recombinant relaxin-2 (serelaxin), which is costly and laborious to produce .
B7-33 acts on the relaxin receptor RXFP1 but is described as a functionally selective agonist: it engages some of the receptor's signalling pathways (notably ERK1/2 phosphorylation) while only weakly stimulating others such as cAMP . Published work on it consists of cell, mouse and rat studies of vascular function, cardiac remodelling and fibrosis . It is not an approved medicine, and no human clinical trial has been published.
It appears in peptide-vendor catalogues in the recovery and tissue-repair category, but the sources reviewed contain no material on how looksmaxxing communities discuss it, and its relevance to appearance is indirect (scarring and fibrosis are among the processes studied).

name: PE-22-28

angle.text: PE-22-28 is a spadin-derived peptide researched in rodents as a fast-acting antidepressant, and some peptide users discuss it for mood and mental sharpness. Human data are absent and no direct appearance use is documented.

summary: A spadin-derived peptide studied in rodents as a fast-acting antidepressant; no human data and no appearance use documented.
note: Rodent data only; unapproved research peptide.
currentQuick:
PE-22-28 is a short peptide trimmed down from spadin, a natural fragment that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel. It was designed to last longer and act more strongly than spadin.
The evidence is limited to mouse and rat experiments on depression-like behaviour. No human trials have been published.
How it works: It inhibits the TREK-1 channel, which helps set neurons' resting potential; blocking it is proposed to produce antidepressant-like effects.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unknown. It is not approved for any use and is available only as a research chemical.
deepLead:
PE-22-28 is a synthetic seven-residue peptide (Gly-Val-Ser-Trp-Gly-Leu-Arg) derived from spadin, an endogenous peptide fragment of the sortilin propeptide that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel . It was designed as a shorter, more potent and more stable analogue of spadin for antidepressant research.
In rodent experiments it has produced antidepressant-like effects after short dosing periods, and it has been reported to last longer in vivo than spadin . No human clinical trial has been published, and it is not an approved medicine. It is categorised in this wiki as a mood-related research peptide; the sources reviewed contain no community discussion of appearance uses.

name: PNC-27

angle.text: PNC-27 is a p53-derived peptide that kills cancer cells in laboratory studies and is sold as a research chemical, with longevity-minded users interested in it. No human trials exist and no appearance use is documented.

summary: A p53-derived peptide shown to lyse cancer cells in lab studies; no human trials, sold only as a research chemical.
note: Cell-line data only; no human safety or efficacy data.
currentQuick:
PNC-27 fuses a piece of the p53 tumour-suppressor protein to a cell-penetrating sequence. In lab experiments it is reported to rupture cancer cells while sparing normal ones.
The evidence is entirely preclinical. No human trial results are published, and no appearance use is documented in the sources reviewed.
How it works: It is reported to bind HDM-2 protein displayed on cancer-cell membranes and to form pores that cause the cell to burst.
Risks and caveats: Human safety is unstudied. It is not an approved drug; it is sold as a research chemical.
deepLead:
PNC-27 is a 32-residue chimeric peptide that joins a segment of the p53 tumour-suppressor protein (residues 12-26, the region that binds HDM-2/MDM2) to a membrane-penetrating sequence . In laboratory studies its authors report that it kills cancer cells, but not normal cells, by binding HDM-2 on the cancer-cell membrane and forming pores that lyse the cell .
All published evidence is from cell lines and laboratory models; no human clinical trial has been published. It is sold by research-peptide vendors and is not an approved medicine. The sources reviewed contain no documented looksmaxxing-community discussion; it is listed under longevity-oriented peptides.

name: Erythropoietin

angle.text: Erythropoietin is a kidney hormone and anaemia drug used for endurance doping, and some physique users discuss it for stamina and recovery capacity in training. Its performance effects are studied in endurance athletes; a direct effect on muscle or appearance is untested.

summary: A kidney hormone and anaemia drug used for endurance doping; indirect link to appearance, with serious cardiovascular warnings.
note: Prescription drug banned in sport; linked to cardiovascular events in some patient groups.
currentQuick:
Erythropoietin is the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. Injectable versions treat anaemia in kidney disease and chemotherapy patients.
It is known mostly as an endurance-sport doping agent. The sources reviewed describe clinical trials in anaemic patients and none aimed at appearance.
How it works: It binds the EPO receptor on red-cell precursors, activating JAK2 signalling to increase red blood cell production. The body releases it more when oxygen is low.
Risks and caveats: It is an Rx-only drug. Reported risks in patients include cardiovascular events and increased mortality in some groups; it is banned in competitive sport.
deepLead:
Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone made mainly by the kidneys in response to low oxygen; it stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. Its gene is switched on by hypoxia-inducible factors, and it signals through the EPO receptor and JAK2 .
Recombinant human EPO (epoetin alfa, first approved by the US FDA in 1989 according to Grokipedia) is used to treat anaemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-related anaemia . In sport and fitness communities it is known as an endurance-boosting performance drug because raising red cell mass increases oxygen-carrying capacity. Its relevance to appearance is indirect, via the muscle and body-composition culture in which it is sometimes mentioned.
Beyond erythropoiesis, laboratory research has examined EPO as a neuroprotective agent, reporting that it crosses the blood-brain barrier in animals and reduces ischaemic brain injury . Grokipedia notes that medical use has raised safety concerns, including increased mortality and serious cardiovascular events in some patient groups .

name: Abaloparatide

angle.text: Abaloparatide is an approved osteoporosis bone-builder that forum users speculate about alongside bonesmashing, orthodontics and limb lengthening for facial structure and height. It has been studied for fracture risk in osteoporosis; no trials address facial bone or appearance.

summary: An approved osteoporosis bone-builder that forums speculate about for bonesmashing and lengthening; no appearance trials exist.
note: Label warns of osteosarcoma risk and advises against use with open growth plates.
currentQuick:
Abaloparatide is a prescription injectable that stimulates bone formation. It is approved for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men, based on trials that reduced fractures.
Looksmaxxing forums discuss it for bonesmashing, puberty and limb lengthening. No published study tests it for those goals.
How it works: It activates the PTH1 receptor, increasing osteoblast activity and new bone formation, a pattern described as bone-anabolic.
Risks and caveats: The label lists osteosarcoma risk, low blood pressure on standing, high calcium, and allergic reactions, and advises avoiding it with open growth plates. It is Rx-only.
deepLead:
Abaloparatide (brand name Tymlos) is a synthetic 34-amino-acid analogue of parathyroid hormone-related protein, PTHrP(1-34), approved in the United States for osteoporosis. Its US label covers postmenopausal women at high fracture risk and men with osteoporosis at high risk, as an injectable bone-forming (anabolic) drug .
The pivotal phase 3 ACTIVE trial reported that abaloparatide reduced new vertebral fractures versus placebo in postmenopausal women . Its approved use is for people with osteoporosis; it is not approved for height, skull, jaw or other appearance purposes.
On looksmax.org, abaloparatide and the related drug teriparatide are discussed in threads about bone density, bonesmashing, puberty and limb lengthening. These discussions are theoretical or anecdotal; no published study has tested it for those goals. The label carries warnings including osteosarcoma risk avoidance in patients with open epiphyses .

name: Salmon calcitonin

angle.text: Salmon calcitonin is used for Paget's disease and high blood calcium, and bone-focused readers mention it as a way to slow bone loss. It has no documented appearance use and is not studied for facial structure.

summary: A fish-derived calcitonin used for Paget's disease and hypercalcaemia; it slows bone loss and has no documented appearance use.
note: Label warns of anaphylaxis, hypocalcaemia and a possible malignancy signal.
currentQuick:
Salmon calcitonin is a prescription peptide that slows bone breakdown. Doctors use it for Paget's disease of bone, high blood calcium and, when other drugs are unsuitable, postmenopausal osteoporosis.
No source reviewed shows looksmaxxing use or tests it for appearance.
How it works: It activates calcitonin receptors on bone-resorbing osteoclasts, reducing bone breakdown and calcium release.
Risks and caveats: The label lists anaphylaxis, low calcium, nausea, flushing and a possible increased malignancy risk. It is Rx-only.
deepLead:
Salmon calcitonin is a synthetic form of calcitonin, a 32-amino-acid peptide hormone made by thyroid C cells that lowers blood calcium by inhibiting bone resorption. The salmon version differs from the human sequence at many positions and is reported to be more potent and longer acting .
The US prescribing label for calcitonin salmon injection lists indications for symptomatic Paget's disease of bone, hypercalcaemia, and postmenopausal osteoporosis when alternatives are unsuitable, noting that fracture-reduction efficacy has not been demonstrated for osteoporosis . It is a bone-resorption inhibitor rather than a bone-building agent. The sources reviewed contain no documented looksmaxxing-community use or appearance-related studies.

name: Osteocalcin

angle.text: Osteocalcin is a bone-made protein and proposed hormone, and bone-focused readers connect it to bone strength and metabolism. It is studied as a marker of bone formation and for metabolic effects; no looks-related use has been tested in humans.

summary: A bone-made protein and proposed hormone studied for bone and metabolism; no looks-related use has been tested in humans.
note: Endogenous protein; no published trials of it as an appearance intervention.
currentQuick:
Osteocalcin is a protein made by bone-building cells. Doctors use its blood level as a marker of how actively bone is being formed.
Since 2007, mouse studies have proposed that it also acts as a hormone on insulin, muscle and testosterone. Human relevance is still being investigated, and no studies test it for appearance.
How it works: Osteoblasts secrete it, and vitamin K-dependent carboxylation lets it bind calcium in bone. The uncarboxylated form is proposed to signal through receptors such as GPRC6A and GPR158 in animal experiments.
Risks and caveats: It is not a marketed product, and the sources describe no approved therapeutic use or safety data for administering it. Human studies reviewed measure it as a marker rather than as a treatment.
deepLead:
Osteocalcin (gene BGLAP) is a small, 49-amino-acid protein made by bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) and found in bone and dentin. Its synthesis and calcium binding depend on vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, and its blood level is widely used as a marker of bone formation.
Since 2007 it has also been studied as a possible bone-derived hormone. Experiments in mice reported that the skeleton influences insulin secretion and energy metabolism through the uncarboxylated form of the protein. Researchers have also reported effects on muscle, testosterone production and the brain in animal studies.
Osteocalcin is an endogenous protein rather than a product sold for appearance purposes. The sources reviewed describe no approved therapeutic use and no published trial testing osteocalcin itself as an intervention for looks, body composition or bone growth.

name: Irisin

angle.text: Irisin is a proposed exercise hormone that fat-loss readers cite as a way exercise might brown fat and raise energy expenditure. The browning finding comes from mice; human evidence is thin and disputed.

summary: A proposed exercise hormone from muscle; mouse fat-browning findings are intriguing but human evidence is thin and disputed.
note: Endogenous protein; existence and measurement in humans have been debated; no approved use.
currentQuick:
Irisin is a protein proposed in 2012 to be released by exercising muscle and to turn white fat toward a brown-fat-like, heat-producing state in mice.
The idea was widely covered, but researchers have disputed how reliably irisin can be measured in people. No trials show irisin as a way to lose fat or change appearance.
How it works: It is cleaved from the membrane protein FNDC5, whose production rises with muscle PGC-1-alpha. Cell and animal studies propose signalling through alpha-V integrin receptors and p38/ERK pathways.
Risks and caveats: No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it. Human studies reviewed mainly measure blood levels.
deepLead:
Irisin is a protein fragment cleaved from FNDC5 (fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5) and was proposed in 2012 as a hormone released by muscle during exercise. Boström and colleagues reported in Nature that it was PGC-1-alpha-dependent and drove brown-fat-like changes in white fat tissue in mice.
The proposal attracted wide attention for possible links to weight loss and diabetes prevention, and it also drew sustained scepticism about whether irisin exists in meaningful circulating amounts in humans and whether commercial assays measure it reliably.
Irisin is an endogenous protein. The sources reviewed describe no approved drug, and human evidence is largely observational measurement of blood levels.

name: Adropin

angle.text: Adropin is a liver and brain peptide linked in mice to fat and glucose metabolism, and fat-loss readers discuss it as a possible metabolic lever. Human data are blood-level associations only; appearance use is untested.

summary: A liver and brain peptide linked to fat metabolism in mice; human data are blood-level associations only.
note: Endogenous peptide; no approved use or human treatment trials found.
currentQuick:
Adropin is a small peptide made mostly in the liver and brain. In mice, low levels go with more body fat and insulin resistance, and giving it improved glucose handling.
In people, lower blood levels have been associated with obesity and heart disease, but no trials test adropin as a way to change body fat or appearance.
How it works: It is cleaved from the ENHO gene product, and its expression follows feeding and the body clock. The receptor is not fully established; GPR19 has been proposed.
Risks and caveats: No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.
deepLead:
Adropin is a 76-amino-acid peptide encoded by the ENHO gene, reported in 2008 in Cell Metabolism as a secreted factor linking dietary macronutrient intake with energy homeostasis and lipid metabolism in mice. Its name derives from Latin words for 'set fire to' and 'fat'.
It is made mainly in the liver and brain. Animal studies report effects on glucose tolerance, fat use, endothelial function and physical activity, while human data consist mostly of blood-level associations with obesity, ageing and cardiometabolic disease.
Adropin is an endogenous peptide. The sources reviewed describe no approved therapeutic use.

name: Asprosin

chain: Blocking it might ease weight gain
angle.text: Asprosin is a fat-derived fasting hormone that raises glucose and appetite in mice, and fat-loss readers follow it as a possible appetite target. High levels track with obesity; no appearance use exists.

summary: A fat-derived fasting hormone that raises glucose and appetite in mice; high levels track with obesity but no appearance use exists.
note: Endogenous hormone; human data are observational; no approved product.
currentQuick:
Asprosin is a hormone released from fat tissue during fasting. In mice it tells the liver to release glucose and the brain to increase appetite.
People with obesity or diabetes tend to have higher levels, while people with a rare syndrome of low asprosin are extremely lean. No studies test it for appearance.
How it works: It is cleaved from fibrillin-1 by furin. Reported receptors include OLFR734/OR4M1 in the liver and PTPRD in the brain; antibodies against it lowered weight in mouse models.
Risks and caveats: No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering or blocking it are described in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Asprosin is a fasting-induced protein hormone cleaved from fibrillin-1 (encoded by FBN1) and released mainly from white fat. It was described in 2016 by Atul Chopra's group at Baylor College of Medicine as raising blood glucose during fasting, and in 2017 as stimulating appetite through the brain.
Blood levels of asprosin are reported to be higher in people with obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. People with a rare inherited condition that lowers asprosin (marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome) are very lean.
Asprosin is an endogenous hormone. The sources reviewed describe antibody-based approaches that lower it in mice, but no approved product.

name: Obestatin

angle.text: Obestatin is a ghrelin-gene peptide first reported to curb appetite, which led fat-loss readers to see it as a possible diet aid. Both its appetite effect and its receptor remain disputed, and appearance use is untested.

summary: A ghrelin-gene peptide first reported to curb appetite; both that effect and its receptor remain disputed.
note: Endogenous peptide; appetite effect and receptor disputed; no human treatment trials found.
currentQuick:
Obestatin is a peptide made from the same gene as the hunger hormone ghrelin. A 2005 paper said it reduced appetite in rodents.
Other labs could not confirm the appetite effect, and its proposed receptor was later called into question. No studies test it for weight or appearance in people.
How it works: It is derived from the ghrelin precursor. GPR39 was proposed as its receptor but later work found that GPR39 responds to zinc instead.
Risks and caveats: No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.
deepLead:
Obestatin is a 23-residue peptide encoded by the same gene as ghrelin. It was reported in Science in 2005 as opposing ghrelin's effects on food intake, and it was found through computer analysis of genome sequences.
Its reported appetite-suppressing effect and its receptor have both been disputed. Later studies found that GPR39, first proposed as its receptor, responds to zinc ions but not obestatin, and some groups could not reproduce its effects on food intake.
Obestatin is an endogenous peptide. The sources reviewed describe no approved use and no trial of it as a treatment.

name: Limostatin

angle.text: Limostatin is a fruit-fly hormone that suppresses insulin during fasting, and metabolism-minded readers cite it as a model for how fasting signals fat handling. It has been studied only in insects, with no human data.

summary: A fruit-fly hormone that switches insulin down during fasting; studied only in insects, with no human data.
note: Fly-only research; no human studies exist.
currentQuick:
Limostatin is a signalling peptide discovered in fruit flies. When food is scarce, it tells insulin-producing cells to release less insulin.
It appears in fat-loss and metabolism peptide lists because of this insulin-lowering role, but the published work is confined to flies and laboratory models.
How it works: In flies, gut endocrine cells release limostatin during nutrient restriction, and it acts on insulin-producing cells to suppress insulin production and secretion.[1]
Risks and caveats: No human safety or efficacy data have been published. Flies lacking limostatin developed high insulin, low blood sugar and excess fat, but this has not been tested in people.[1]
deepLead:
Limostatin (Lst) is a peptide hormone first identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. It is released from gut-associated endocrine cells when nutrients are scarce and suppresses the production and secretion of insulin-like peptides, which made it the first well-characterised example of a "decretin", a fasting-induced hormone that opposes insulin.
All published work on limostatin consists of insect or cell-based laboratory research. Flies lacking the gene showed high insulin levels, low blood sugar and extra body fat in the original 2015 study. No human trial of limostatin or a limostatin-based product has been reported, and no source reviewed for this article documents its use for appearance or body-composition goals in humans.

name: Alamandine

angle.text: Alamandine is a blood-pressure-regulating peptide of the renin-angiotensin system, discussed by longevity-minded readers for cardiovascular and tissue-protective effects. It has been studied in rodents; no human trials or appearance use exist.

summary: A blood-pressure-regulating peptide of the renin-angiotensin system; interesting cardiovascular biology in rodents, no human trials.
note: Preclinical only; no human therapeutic data.
currentQuick:
Alamandine is a small peptide made in the body as part of the renin-angiotensin system. It was described in 2013 and appears to counterbalance the blood-pressure-raising arm of that system.
Evidence for any effect comes from cell and rodent experiments. It is listed among longevity-category peptides, but no human trials have tested it.
How it works: It is generated by ACE2 from angiotensin A (or from angiotensin-(1-7)) and signals mainly through the MrgD receptor, producing vasorelaxation and anti-fibrotic effects in animals.[1][5]
Risks and caveats: No human safety data exist. Because it influences blood pressure and vascular tone in animals, effects in people are unstudied. It is not an approved drug.
deepLead:
Alamandine is a heptapeptide of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), the hormone network that regulates blood pressure, fluid and electrolyte balance. It was characterised in 2013 and is formed from angiotensin A by ACE2, or directly from angiotensin-(1-7).
It acts mainly through the MrgD receptor and, in laboratory studies, produces effects that oppose those of angiotensin II, such as vasorelaxation and protection against cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis in animals. Published work is preclinical; no human clinical trial of alamandine as a treatment was found, and no source reviewed documents appearance-related use.

name: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone

angle.text: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone sits at the top of the thyroid axis, and hormone-minded readers discuss it for thyroid, mood and energy effects. Human studies outside diagnostics are small and dated; appearance use is untested.

summary: The hypothalamic hormone that tells the pituitary to make TSH; a brain-active peptide with only small, dated human studies outside diagnostics.
note: Short half-life; non-endocrine uses remain investigational.
currentQuick:
TRH is a three-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus. It signals the pituitary to release TSH and prolactin, which control the thyroid.
It appears in recovery-category peptide lists because of brain effects seen in research, but human data beyond diagnostic testing are small and old.
How it works: TRH binds receptors on pituitary thyrotroph cells to trigger TSH release, and is cleared within minutes; in the brain it influences arousal and neurotransmitter release.[8][11]
Risks and caveats: Reported effects of injected TRH include nausea, flushing and a mild blood pressure rise.[11] Because it raises TSH and prolactin, endocrine effects are expected. It has not been established as a treatment for the conditions studied.
deepLead:
Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH, also thyroliberin; the pharmaceutical form is protirelin) is a tripeptide, pyroglutamyl-histidyl-proline amide, made mainly by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus. It stimulates the pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and prolactin, and so sits at the top of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.
TRH was the first hypothalamic releasing hormone to be structurally identified, in 1969, and its discoverers shared the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Beyond its endocrine role it acts in the brain, where it has been studied for effects on wakefulness, seizures, mood and neurological disease. Clinical use has been mainly diagnostic, and trials of TRH for other conditions have been small or inconclusive. No source reviewed documents an established appearance-related use.
